Unit 3 • HL

Recursive Problem Solving

Introduction

How can a problem solve itself?

This unit focuses on Self-Reference and Decomposition. You will learn how to write functions that call themselves to solve complex problems like sorting (Quicksort) and tree traversal. You will start by tracing the Runtime Stack and finish by mastering the Divide and Conquer strategy.

You'll begin with the anatomy of a recursive method (Base Case vs General Case). Then you'll visualize memory using the Call Stack (Winding/Unwinding), and apply this logic to implement efficient algorithms like Quicksort.

The Anatomy of Recursion

A recursive method has two parts. Without both, it fails:

  • Base Case: The stopping condition (e.g., if n == 0). Stops the infinite loop.
  • General (Recursive) Case: The logic that calls the method again with a smaller input (e.g., return n + Sum(n-1)).

The Call Stack (Memory)

How does the computer remember where it was? It uses a Stack.

  • Winding (Push): Adding a new "Frame" to the stack for each call.
  • Unwinding (Pop): When the Base Case is hit, frames pop off, returning values back up the chain.

Divide & Conquer (Sorting)

Recursion is powerful for breaking big problems into small ones.

  • Quicksort: Pick a pivot, partition the list (smaller left, bigger right), then recurse on both sides.
  • Merge Sort: Split the list in half recursively until size 1, then merge them back in order.

Key Terminology
TermDefinition
RecursionA programming technique where a function calls itself to solve a problem.
Base CaseThe condition that stops the recursion (prevents an infinite loop).
Recursive StepThe part of the function where it calls itself with a modified (usually smaller) parameter.
Call StackA memory structure that stores 'Stack Frames' for each active function call (tracks local logic).
Stack OverflowA fatal error that occurs when the Call Stack runs out of memory (usually due to a missing Base Case).
Stack FrameA section of the stack dedicated to a single function call, storing its arguments, return address, and local variables.
PivotThe element in Quicksort used to partition the array.

Common Misconceptions

Recursion is just a Loop

It feels like a loop, but it eats memory! Each 'loop' adds a new frame to the Stack. An infinite recursion crashes execution; an infinite loop just hangs.

The Function Stops at Base Case

No! That's just the half-way point. The function must then 'Unwind' all the way back up the stack to finish.

Variables are Shared

Thinking 'n' is the same variable in every call. Each recursive call has its own separate copy of 'n'.

  • B2.4.4 Recursion Definition

Real-World Uses

  • File System Traversal (folders inside folders)
  • Pathfinding (Mazes)
  • Fractals (Sierpinski Triangle)
  • Game Logic (Chess AI looking ahead)
  • Processing nested data (JSON/XML)

Think Deeper

"Why use Recursion?" If Iteration (Loops) is faster and uses less memory, why do we use Recursion? Is code readability and 'elegance' worth the performance cost?
